",a(r.p,{children:[e(r.strong,{children:"Spring Boot 3.x and Java 21 vs lighter stacks"}),"
Spring Boot buys a mature, batteries-included ecosystem: Spring Security handling JWT, Springdoc generating Swagger UI, and a consistent configuration model with almost no glue code. The cost is real — JVM memory footprint, startup time, and plenty of ceremonial code (DTOs, mappers, layer interfaces) that a Go or Node service would not need. At the scale of a portfolio API, developer velocity and type safety outweigh the resource overhead."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[e(r.strong,{children:"Spring Data JPA (Hibernate) vs raw SQL"}),"
Repository interfaces and entity relationships keep a 20-plus-table relational model manageable, and the persistence code stays database-agnostic. The price is a leaky abstraction: lazy-loading pitfalls, N+1 query risk on relationships like order items and reviews, and little visibility into the SQL Hibernate actually emits. For CRUD-heavy commerce flows that is an acceptable trade; hand-tuned SQL only pays off under heavy read load."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[e(r.strong,{children:"PostgreSQL vs a document store"}),"
An e-commerce schema spanning users, merchants, products, carts, orders, and transactions is fundamentally relational — an order must atomically bind a user, its order items, and a shipping address, and referential integrity should be enforced by the database rather than application code. The trade-off is schema rigidity: every new attribute means a migration, and horizontal scaling is harder than with documents. Consistency matters more here than flexibility."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[e(r.strong,{children:"JWT with refresh tokens vs server sessions"}),"
Stateless JWTs keep the API horizontally scalable with no session store, and the dedicated refresh-token table allows token rotation and per-user revocation paths. The cost is that security changes such as logout-everywhere or role downgrades take effect only as fast as token expiry, and client-side token handling is more complex than a cookie session. For a stateless public API this remains the standard, defensible choice."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[e(r.strong,{children:"Single deployable vs microservices"}),"
Auth, catalog, cart, orders, reviews, and merchant management all live in one process over one database, which keeps transactional boundaries trivial and deployment a single jar. What is given up is independent scaling and fault isolation — a burst of review writes pressures the same pool as checkout. Splitting would only pay off at team and traffic scales this project does not operate at."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[e(r.strong,{children:"Stock integrity on checkout (the core domain risk)"}),"
Products carry a countInStock column that order fulfillment must decrement. The honest risk is the race: two concurrent checkouts reading the same stock can oversell unless the decrement runs inside the same transaction as order creation, ideally as a conditional update that only applies when stock is sufficient rather than a read-then-write. Application-level checks alone are the cheapest implementation and the easiest one to break under load."]}),"

",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"Spring Boot on the JVM vs lighter stacks"}),"
For a payment API the argument is less about raw throughput and more about correctness tooling: declarative transactions, a mature security filter chain, and a consistent configuration model reduce the chance of hand-rolled mistakes in money paths. The trade is a heavyweight runtime — hundreds of megabytes of RAM before serving the first request — and configuration ceremony that Go or Node would not impose. For a system whose bottleneck is trust rather than speed, that trade is easy to defend."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"Spring Data JPA (Hibernate) over hand-written SQL"}),"
Entities and repositories keep persistence consistent across users, cards, merchants, and the movement tables, and transactional method boundaries come nearly free. The cost: Hibernate hides the exact SQL and locking behavior, which is precisely where payment bugs live — a missing lock on a balance row or an unintended flush order is invisible at the code level. Worth it at this scale, but it demands discipline around transaction boundaries."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"PostgreSQL as the ledger"}),"
Every movement — topup, transfer, withdrawal, merchant payment — is its own row with a UUID reference number and a status column, which is the right shape for an audit trail: foreign keys tie movements to cards, and ACID commits make a half-applied transfer impossible at the storage layer. The trade-off is write amplification (each balance change produces movement rows plus a saldo update) and a schema that must be migrated carefully, because financial columns are the hardest thing in the system to change."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"JWT plus RBAC in a money API"}),"
Stateless tokens scale horizontally and keep the contract clean for third-party integrators using merchant API keys, while role checks gate the sensitive admin, merchant, and user endpoints. The honest weakness: bearer tokens cannot be instantly revoked, and in a payment system a leaked token with minutes of validity is a bigger deal than on a content site. Refresh-token rotation narrows the window; closing it requires token introspection or very short TTLs, both of which cost infrastructure."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"One deployable vs service-per-domain"}),"
Auth, cards, saldo, topups, transfers, withdrawals, and merchants run in a single Spring Boot process, so a transfer can debit one card and credit another inside one local database transaction — the exact operation that becomes a saga once services split. The cost is a shared failure domain and no per-domain scaling, acceptable while the whole system fits one database."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"Idempotency and balance consistency (the core domain risk)"}),"
Each operation carries a unique reference — topup_no, withdraw_no, transfer_no, transaction_no — which is the foundation for idempotent retries instead of double charges. What the implementation still has to guarantee is conditional balance mutation: saldo updates need a row lock or an atomic compare-and-update that rejects insufficient funds, because two concurrent transfers against one card will race otherwise. The status columns also imply a reconciliation story for movements stuck in a non-final state — a defined retry or expiry path, not just a row that sits there."]}),"

",e(i.h2,{id:"technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:e(i.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:"Technical Decisions & Trade-offs"})}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"Spring Boot and the JVM vs lighter stacks"}),"
A POS backend is CRUD plus transactions, which is exactly the workload Spring Boot is built for: Spring Security for the admin, merchant, and cashier role model, Springdoc for the Swagger UI a register client would be developed against, and one consistent repository layer. The cost is a JVM process idling at a memory level a Go binary would not reach, plus generous boilerplate. For a back-office API where correctness and documentation matter more than cold starts, the trade is reasonable."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"Spring Data JPA (Hibernate) vs SQL-first development"}),"
Entities mirror the schema — merchants, cashiers, products, orders, order items, transactions — and repositories remove most hand-written persistence code. The trade-off is that Hibernate decides when stock decrements and totals actually hit the database, and a wrong flush order can silently change which value wins. Keeping writes short and explicitly transactional is the discipline that makes the abstraction safe here."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"PostgreSQL vs lighter storage options"}),"
Checkout is a multi-table write: create the order, decompose order items, record a transaction with amount and change, all under one ACID commit. PostgreSQL also enforces the foreign keys between merchants, cashiers, products, and orders that keep per-merchant reporting trustworthy. The cost is running and backing up a real database server where an embedded store would be simpler — justified, because sales records are exactly the data you cannot afford to lose or corrupt."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"JWT roles on shared register hardware"}),"
Stateless tokens fit POS clients that reconnect often and should not need server-side session affinity, and RBAC keeps a cashier token away from merchant and admin endpoints. The weak spot is revocation: a cashier token stays valid until expiry even if the employee is deactivated mid-shift, and refresh tokens only shorten that window when rotation is enforced. For internal staff devices the blast radius is contained, but it is a real limitation to design around."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"Single service vs splitting merchant, catalog, and sales"}),"
Everything from product management to transaction processing runs in one deployable, so an order and its stock update commit atomically in one database transaction — no sagas, no eventual consistency in the checkout path. What is lost is isolation: a heavy admin report can slow the register lane, and the whole API redeploys as one unit. At the scale of a handful of merchants per instance, that is the right trade."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[e(i.strong,{children:"Cash handling and register integrity (the core domain risk)"}),"
Transactions store the paid amount and a computed change amount, which moves cash math into application code — change must be validated against the amount paid inside the same transaction that records the sale, or the till drifts. Attribution matters just as much: every order carries a cashier id so end-of-day reconciliation is possible, but only if voids and failed payments are persisted as first-class records rather than silent edits. A POS that lets a sale and its payment record diverge is worse than one that refuses the sale."]}),"

title: Booking Hotel
excerpt: A hotel booking management system with user authentication, built using Spring Boot and PostgreSQL, running in a Docker environment.
body:
const{Fragment:e,jsx:n,jsxs:i}=arguments[0];function _createMdxContent(a){const o={a:"a",code:"code",em:"em",figure:"figure",h1:"h1",h2:"h2",h3:"h3",li:"li",ol:"ol",p:"p",pre:"pre",span:"span",strong:"strong",ul:"ul",...a.components};return i(e,{children:[n(o.h1,{id:"-booking-hotel",children:n(o.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#-booking-hotel",children:"🏨 Booking Hotel"})}),"
",i(o.p,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"Booking Hotel"})," is a hotel booking management system that includes user authentication and various related features. This application is built with ",n(o.strong,{children:"Spring Boot"})," and uses ",n(o.strong,{children:"PostgreSQL"})," as the main database. The system also provides ",n(o.strong,{children:"OpenAPI"})," documentation and can be easily deployed in a ",n(o.strong,{children:"Docker"})," environment."]}),"
",n(o.h2,{id:"-features",children:n(o.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#-features",children:"✨ Features"})}),"
",i(o.ul,{children:["
",i(o.li,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"Hotel Booking Management"})," – Users can book hotel rooms with multiple available options."]}),"
",i(o.li,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"User Authentication"})," – Supports user registration, login, and account management."]}),"
",i(o.li,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"API Documentation"})," – Uses ",n(o.strong,{children:"OpenAPI"})," for documentation and API exploration."]}),"
",i(o.li,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"Relational Database"})," – Stores user and booking data using ",n(o.strong,{children:"PostgreSQL"}),"."]}),"
",i(o.li,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"Containerized Deployment"})," – Easily deployable with ",n(o.strong,{children:"Docker"}),"."]}),"
"]}),"
",n(o.h2,{id:"business-logic",children:n(o.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#business-logic",children:"Business Logic"})}),"
",i(o.ol,{children:["
",i(o.li,{children:["
",n(o.p,{children:"Sign Up & Login
Users can create an account and log in to access the app."}),"
"]}),"
",i(o.li,{children:["
",n(o.p,{children:"Email Verification
After signing up, users must verify their email address to activate their account."}),"
"]}),"
",i(o.li,{children:["
",n(o.p,{children:"Room Booking
Users can browse and book available hotel rooms."}),"
"]}),"
",i(o.li,{children:["
",n(o.p,{children:"Check-in & Check-out
When arriving at the hotel, users can check in digitally.
Upon departure, they can check out through the app."}),"
"]}),"
",i(o.li,{children:["
",n(o.p,{children:"Forgot Password
If users forget their password, they can reset it via a link sent to their email."}),"
"]}),"
",i(o.li,{children:["
",n(o.p,{children:"Room Management (Admin Only)
Admins can add, update, or remove rooms from the system."}),"
"]}),"
"]}),"
",n(o.h2,{id:"technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:n(o.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:"Technical Decisions & Trade-offs"})}),"
",i(o.p,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"Spring Boot + JVM vs lighter stacks (Go, Node.js)"}),"
Chosen for its mature ecosystem: Spring Security handles registration/login/verification with little custom code, and OpenAPI support ships out of the box. The cost is a heavier runtime — JVM startup time and memory footprint are much larger than a Go/Node service, and boilerplate (DTOs, mappers, config classes) grows quickly. For this scale that's a fine trade; the payoff in developer velocity and type safety wins."]}),"
",i(o.p,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"PostgreSQL (relational) vs NoSQL"}),"
A booking system fundamentally needs ACID transactions and referential integrity: a booking must atomically link user ↔ room ↔ date range, and availability checks are relational queries (date-range overlap). A document store would make the consistency logic ad-hoc. The trade-off is a rigid schema — every new room type or status means a migration — and it doesn't scale horizontally the way a document store can. At this data volume, consistency wins."]}),"
",n(o.p,{children:n(o.strong,{children:"Preventing double-booking (the core domain trade-off)"})}),"
",i(o.ul,{children:["
",i(o.li,{children:[n(o.em,{children:"Pessimistic locking"})," (",n(o.code,{children:"SELECT ... FOR UPDATE"})," on the room row): simple and safe, but serialized — throughput collapses when many users fight for the same room."]}),"
",i(o.li,{children:[n(o.em,{children:"Optimistic locking"}),' (version column on room/availability): high throughput, no blocking, but contended requests fail and must retry — the client has to handle "someone just took this room" gracefully.']}),"
",i(o.li,{children:["Last line of defense either way: a ",n(o.em,{children:"unique constraint"})," on the room + overlapping date range, so the database itself rejects a duplicate even if application logic has a race. I leaned toward optimistic with the unique constraint as a backstop, prioritizing throughput over simplicity."]}),"
"]}),"
",i(o.p,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"Monolith vs microservices"}),"
Auth, booking, and room management live in one Spring Boot app. That keeps local development trivial (one ",n(o.code,{children:"docker-compose up"}),"), with a single deployable and simple transactional boundaries. The costs: no independent scaling (the whole app scales as one unit), shared failure domain, and coarser team boundaries. At this scope that's the right call — the overhead of inter-service communication (network, serialization, distributed transactions) would exceed the benefit."]}),"
",i(o.p,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"Docker / docker-compose deployment"}),'
Reproducible environment, one-command setup. The trade-off: a compose stack is still a single-node story — no load balancer, auto-scaling, or CI/CD pipeline behind it. It's "containerized" but not "production-grade infrastructure."']}),"
",i(o.p,{children:[n(o.strong,{children:"Email-based verification & password reset"}),"
Standard UX, but it outsources availability to the email pipeline (deliverability, SPF/DKIM, spam folders). The security trade-off lives in token design: reset/verification links must be ",n(o.em,{children:"random, single-use, and short-lived"})," (stored hashed, not in plain text), otherwise a leaked or guessed link hands over the account."]}),"

obvious alternative — ",n(i.code,{children:"tcpdump"}),"-style sniffing — copies every packet to user space, which burns CPU and starts dropping packets under load. eBPF runs the filter logic inside the kernel: each packet costs only a handful of instructions, and the verifier guarantees the program terminates (no unbounded loops, no arbitrary memory access), which is why it's far safer than a kernel module. The price of that safety: BPF programs are hard to debug, must satisfy the verifier's constraints, and need kernel 4.9+ with matching headers. That's a real portability cost, not a cosmetic one."]})," ",r(i.p,{children:[n(i.strong,{children:"Ring buffer vs BPF map for event transport"})," The kernel→user channel uses a ring buffer: the kernel side just appends, the Go consumer pulls at its own pace, and under back-pressure the kernel overwrites the oldest events instead of blocking the packet path — monitoring must never slow down the traffic it's observing. The trade-off: sustained high event rates cause silent overruns, so the user-space side must track the overrun counter (",n(i.code,{children:"ebpf_events_total"}),") as a first-class signal. A per-CPU hash map would be more loss-resistant but adds aggregation complexity and overhead we didn't need."]})," ",r(i.p,{children:[n(i.strong,{children:"Keeping the eBPF program deliberately thin"})," The kernel program only captures a fixed event struct (PID, IPs, query type, byte counters) and does no formatting or labelling. BPF code is painful to iterate on (compile, load, verifier errors), so every bit of logic that can live in Go belongs in Go. The trade-off: more data crosses the kernel/user boundary and user-space aggregation has to be fast enough — which is exactly where the Go consumer shines (goroutines + channel pipeline, cheap pre-allocated buffers)."]})," ",r(i.p,{children:[n(i.strong,{children:"Full capture vs sampling"}),' Capturing every DNS query and every byte counter means no rare events are missed — important for this use case, where "one weird query from PID X" is often the interesting signal. The cost is that metrics volume grows with traffic, so downstream (Prometheus scrape + Grafana) becomes the bottleneck long before the kernel side does. Sampling would have kept the cost flat but would have biased the statistics toward the loud and the large.']})," ",r(i.p,{children:[n(i.strong,{children:"Go for the user-space agent"})," Go was chosen mainly for the ",n(i.code,{children:"cilium/ebpf"}),' library (a first-class, actively maintained eBPF loader) and for producing a single static binary — an agent that has to run on many machines should not drag along a runtime. FastAPI was chosen due to its high performance and its syntax similarity to Express.js."]}),"
",n(t.h2,{id:"-features",children:n(t.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#-features",children:"✨ Features"})}),"
",a(t.ul,{children:["

",a(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Frontend with React and Tailwind CSS"})," 🖥️🌊 – Modern UI with a responsive design."]}),"
",a(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"JWT Authentication"})," 🔐 – Secure user authentication system."]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.h2,{id:"-technologies-used",children:n(t.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#-technologies-used",children:"🛠 Technologies Used"})}),"
",a(t.ul,{children:["
",a(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"FastAPI"})," 🚀 – High-performance web framework for building APIs."]}),"
",a(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"React.js"})," ⚛️ – Modern frontend library for dynamic UI."]}),"
",a(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"PostgreSQL"})," 🗃️ – Relational database management system."]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.h2,{id:"️-technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:n(t.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#️-technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:"⚖️ Technical Decisions & Trade-offs"})}),"
",a(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"FastAPI vs Django / Flask"}),"
FastAPI gives you ASGI (true async), Pydantic-validated request/response models, and auto-generated OpenAPI docs for free — a good deal for a REST API. The cost: it's an API framework, not a full web framework, so you assemble auth, admin, and ORM wiring yourself (Django ships all three out of the box). For a headless backend in front of a React app, that's the right trade — you're not paying for web-page machinery you don't use."]}),"
",a(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"PostgreSQL for e-commerce"}),"
An e-commerce domain (products, carts, orders, inventory) is squarely relational: order/stock changes must be atomic, or you oversell. ACID transactions and FK integrity are the payoff. The cost is a fixed schema — every catalog change is a migration, and it won't scale horizontally the way a document store can. At this data volume, that's a non-issue."]}),"
",a(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"JWT over session cookies"}),"
JWTs are stateless: no server-side session store, so any replica can verify any request — clean for a horizontally scaled API. The honest trade-offs: a leaked access token is valid until it expires (no instant revocation without a blacklist or short expiry + refresh-token rotation), and claims are small — you can't store much in the token, so it just carries identity. The standard mitigation is short-lived access tokens + rotating refresh tokens."]}),"
",a(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"React SPA + Tailwind for the frontend"}),"
A fully client-side app gives fast interactions and a clean component model; Tailwind keeps styling consistent without a CSS framework's abstraction layer. The costs: no server-rendered HTML, so SEO has to be handled deliberately (and a static SPA behind a headless API has two deployables + CORS to manage, instead of one). For a portfolio-scale storefront that's acceptable; a public high-traffic store would push toward SSR (Next.js) or a partial-island approach."]}),"
",a(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:'Why FastAPI "feels like Express"'}),"
The framework was chosen partly for the familiar mental model: route-driven handlers, dependency injection for auth/middleware, and minimal boilerplate — so the API reads the way an Express router would, but with strict request validation and typed responses underneath."]}),"

title: Ecommerce Fiber with Midtrans and Raja Ongkir
excerpt: An e-commerce application using the Fiber framework for the backend, integrated with Midtrans for payments and Raja Ongkir for shipping.

const{Fragment:e,jsx:n,jsxs:r}=arguments[0];function _createMdxContent(i){const t={a:"a",code:"code",em:"em",h2:"h2",h3:"h3",img:"img",li:"li",ol:"ol",p:"p",strong:"strong",ul:"ul",...i.components};return r(e,{children:[n(t.h2,{id:"-project-description",children:n(t.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#-project-description",children:"🛒 Project Description"})}),"
",r(t.p,{children:["This project is an ",n(t.strong,{children:"e-commerce application"})," built with ",n(t.strong,{children:"Fiber"})," ⚡, a lightweight and fast Go framework for the backend. It integrates two essential services:"]}),"
",r(t.ol,{children:["
",r(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Midtrans"})," 💳 for payment processing."]}),"
",r(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Raja Ongkir"})," 📦 for shipping services."]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.p,{children:"The application provides a seamless shopping experience with a clean and functional user interface, as well as an admin panel for managing products and orders."}),"
",n(t.h3,{id:"-key-features",children:n(t.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#-key-features",children:"✨ Key Features"})}),"
",r(t.ul,{children:["

",r(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Shipping Service"})," 📦: Integrated with ",n(t.strong,{children:"Raja Ongkir"})," to provide reliable shipping solutions."]}),"
",r(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Frontend"})," 🖥️: Modern and responsive user interface."]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.h3,{id:"-technologies-used",children:n(t.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#-technologies-used",children:"🛠 Technologies Used"})}),"
",r(t.ul,{children:["

",r(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Payment"})," 💳: ",n(t.strong,{children:"Midtrans"})]}),"
",r(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Shipping"})," 📦: ",n(t.strong,{children:"Raja Ongkir"})]}),"
",r(t.li,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Frontend"})," 🖥️: ",n(t.strong,{children:"React.js"})," ⚛️, ",n(t.strong,{children:"Bootstrap 5"})," ⚙️, and ",n(t.strong,{children:"Tauri.js"})," 🦀"]}),"
"]}),"
",n(t.h2,{id:"technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:n(t.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:"Technical Decisions & Trade-offs"})}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Go + Fiber"}),"
A single static binary with a tiny footprint, which suits an API server well. The trade-off is that Fiber is built on ",n(t.code,{children:"fasthttp"}),", not the stdlib ",n(t.code,{children:"net/http"}),": Koa-style middleware and speed, but different server semantics (e.g., HTTP/2 support) and an ecosystem that mostly assumes the standard library."]}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"GORM vs raw SQL"}),"
GORM buys dev speed: associations, callbacks, and auto-migration. The costs are reflection overhead, opaque SQL generation (you need the logger to audit what it actually runs), N+1 risk on associations (deliberate ",n(t.code,{children:"Preload"}),"), and auto-migration being fine in dev but something you must not run in production."]}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Outsourcing payment to Midtrans"}),"
You don't build payment infrastructure: PCI compliance, many payment methods, and a sandbox for free. The cost is a dependency on someone else's SLA — and because payment success arrives asynchronously (webhook), the order must sit in a ",n(t.em,{children:"pending"})," state that transitions on notification. That forces idempotent webhook handling (retries and duplicates) plus a reconciliation fallback for callbacks that get lost."]}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"RajaOngkir for shipping rates"}),"
Instant per-route shipping cost without implementing carrier pricing — but a second external dependency (rate limits, API changes), and the rate fetched at cart time can be stale by order confirmation, so it gets re-validated at checkout."]}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Tauri desktop shell around React"}),"
Tauri's Rust shell ships a fraction of an Electron binary's size. The trade-offs: per-OS packaging and signing, and distributing an e-commerce storefront as a desktop app is a demo choice, not a distribution channel. The backend is a separate process, so its URL/CORS must be configured per platform."]}),"

",a(i.p,{children:[n(i.strong,{children:"gRPC + Protobuf vs plain REST between modules"}),"
Typed, versioned contracts; binary + HTTP/2 is lighter and faster than JSON for internal calls; the generated code keeps every consumer compiling against the same schema. The costs: payloads are not human-readable in transit (inspect with ",n(i.code,{children:"grpcurl"})," or the gateway), no browser can call it directly, and schema evolution must stay backward-compatible (add fields, never rename) or every downstream service breaks at once."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[n(i.strong,{children:"REST gateway (Echo) in front of gRPC"}),"
External clients keep a friendly JSON/HTTP surface plus Swaggo-generated docs, while the core logic speaks gRPC. The trade-off: a second code path to maintain, and gRPC status codes have to be mapped to HTTP semantics deliberately — error handling now exists in two dialects."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[n(i.strong,{children:"sqlc vs an ORM"}),"
sqlc generates type-safe Go code from hand-written SQL: no reflection, no magic query building, and the queries are explicit and easy to audit with ",n(i.code,{children:"EXPLAIN"}),". The cost is that every query is written by hand and schema changes need a code-generation step — upfront work that buys the predictable performance the load tests below care about."]}),"
",a(i.p,{children:[n(i.strong,{children:"Goose migrations vs auto-migration"}),"
Version-controlled, ordered migrations: reviewable in PRs and safe to run in production; auto-migration's habit of silently altering (or dropping) columns never applies. ",a(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Django (batteries-included) vs API-first frameworks (FastAPI)"}),"
An inventory tool with a dashboard is exactly Django's sweet spot: the admin panel, ORM, auth, and form validation all ship out of the box, so a working internal app is days, not weeks. The cost of convenience: Django renders server-side HTML pages, so it's not a JSON API — feeding it to a modern SPA later means adding DRF or a second service. You also inherit its conventions, including the synchronous WSGI request model (a fine default, just not the async ceiling of ASGI)."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Django ORM vs raw SQL"}),"
The ORM gives safe, relation-aware queries with no injection risk and minimal boilerplate. The trade-off: generated SQL is opaque until you turn on the query logger, and unguarded relation access causes N+1 queries — which is why an inventory dashboard must be built with ",n(r.code,{children:"select_related"}),"/",n(r.code,{children:"prefetch_related"})," on purpose, not by accident."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Bootstrap for the dashboard UI"}),"
Off-the-shelf tables, forms, and cards are fast to assemble for a dense admin interface. The cost: it looks like every other Bootstrap admin panel — visual identity takes deliberate effort to escape the framework's defaults."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Session-based auth out of the box"}),"
Django's session + auth system works immediately (login, logout, password reset, admin). The trade-off: sessions are server-side state, so scaling to multiple replicas requires shared session storage (Redis or the database); a stateless JWT approach scales more freely but gives up instant revocation."]}),"

Trade-offs"})})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Fourteen microservices vs a modular monolith"})," Each domain (auth, user, role, card, saldo, topup, transfer, …) is a self-contained, micro-deployable Go binary with its own gRPC boundary, which buys fault containment, independent HPA scaling, and teams that can deploy without a global freeze window. The honest cost: 14 deployables plus 11 isolated Redis instances, a Kafka bus, PgBouncer, and a full observability suite is a lot of moving parts for a single local host to run — a modular monolith would give the same domain boundaries with none of the network hops and wiring. This architecture is a bet that scale and team size will justify the overhead."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Synchronous gRPC + asynchronous Kafka, mixed by interaction type"})," Request/response semantics (card lookup, balance check) stay synchronous gRPC: simple, immediate, and typed. Fire-and-forget side effects (email notifications, OLAP ingestion) go through Kafka: consumers can lag, retry, or be offline without blocking the transaction. The trade-off lives at the seams: the sync path has hard dependencies (a slow or dead downstream service stalls the caller unless circuit breakers trip), and the async path is at-least-once — every consumer (email worker, stats writer) must be idempotent, and ordering can only be guaranteed within a partition."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"CQRS-style read path: ClickHouse instead of querying Postgres"}),' Analytics (monthly/yearly volumes, payment-method breakdowns) hit a column-oriented ClickHouse fed by a stats-writer consuming Kafka, keeping heavy aggregations off the OLTP database. The costs: the analytics view is eventually consistent — a just-completed transfer isn't in the dashboard yet — and the pipeline adds real surface area (Kafka topic, writer service, a second database with its own ops). For near-real-time BI that lag is acceptable; for "show me the state of this order right now" it is not.']})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Eleven isolated Redis databases, one per service"})," Namespacing by dedicated database/instance means no cross-service key collisions and independent flush/scale. The price: eleven containers in compose, each carrying its own baseline memory footprint, and cache state that dies with its service unless persisted — isolation is bought with resource duplication."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"PgBouncer between services and PostgreSQL"})," Many concurrent Go services opening raw Postgres sockets quickly exhausts the server's connection limit, so every service talks to a PgBouncer pooler instead. The trade-off: pooling at transaction mode is the safe default, but session-level features (prepared statements, server-side cursors, per-connection state) stop working across the pooler — the query style has to stay pooler-friendly."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Full observability suite (Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger + Pyroscope + Alertmanager)"})," All three pillars plus continuous profiling, wired through OpenTelemetry, means a slow transaction can be followed from the REST edge across gRPC boundaries down to SQL. The cost is a resident footprint of dashboards, exporters, and collectors — heavy for a local box, and the right call only if someone actually operates the dashboards; unmonitored telemetry is just overhead."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Docker Compose (local) + Kubernetes (production) as two first-class targets"}),' Local parity with prod (same service split, HPA manifests, PVCs) keeps "works on my machine" closer to true, and rolling updates + autoscaling come from the orchestrator. The trade-off: two deployment artifacts to keep in sync, and a gap between them is where configuration drift lives — the compose stack and the K8s manifests must be reviewed together on every infra change.']})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"sqlc + Goose for the data layer"})," Type-safe, compiler-checked SQL plus version-ordered migrations: predictable performance and no auto-migration surprises. The cost, repeated from the other Go projects: every query is hand-written and a code-generation step sits between the schema and the code."]})," ",n(r.hr,{})," Trade-offs"})})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Fourteen microservices vs a modular monolith"})," Every financial domain (saldo, topup, transfer, withdraw, …) is a self-contained, micro-deployable Go binary with its own gRPC boundary: fault containment, independent HPA scaling for financial traffic, and no shared-process risk between, say, auth and the ledger. The honest cost: 14 deployables, 11 isolated Redis instances, Kafka, PgBouncer, and a full observability suite is a heavy local stack — a modular monolith would give the same boundaries with none of the wiring. For a payment system the split is a deliberate bet that the critical ledger gets isolation, resourcing, and release cadence of its own."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Synchronous gRPC + asynchronous Kafka, split by interaction type"})," Balance checks and card lookups stay synchronous gRPC: immediate, typed, and easy to reason about. Side effects (emails, OLAP ingestion) flow through Kafka so consumers can lag or restart without blocking a transaction. In a payment context the async trade-off is sharper than anywhere else: Kafka is at-least-once, so a redelivered ",n(r.code,{children:"transfer.created"})," event can double-book a ledger entry unless consumers key on an idempotency token and check before applying — that's the price of decoupling financial side effects."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Optimistic concurrency on the Saldo (balance) service"})," Real-time balance math uses versioned optimistic locks instead of long-held row locks: a transfer reads the balance, applies debit/credit with a ",n(r.code,{children:"WHERE version = N"})," guard, and retries on conflict. The trade-off: under heavy contention on one hot account, retries churn and some requests visibly fail-then-retry, whereas pessimistic locking would serialize them silently. Optimistic is the right call for read-mostly accounts with bursty writes; a truly hot account would need queueing or sharding instead."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"CQRS read path: ClickHouse instead of querying Postgres"}),' Analytics (monthly/yearly volumes, payment-method breakdowns) hit a column-oriented ClickHouse fed asynchronously by the stats-writer, keeping heavy aggregations off the OLTP ledger. The costs: the analytics view lags real time (a just-settled transfer is not yet in the dashboard) and the pipeline adds surface area — a Kafka topic, a writer service, and a second database with its own ops. Acceptable for BI; never use it for "state of this order right now," which must always read the ledger.']})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Eleven isolated Redis databases, one per service"})," Per-service isolation means no cross-service key collisions and independent flush/scale, but eleven containers in compose, each carrying its own baseline memory — isolation bought with resource duplication."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"PgBouncer between services and PostgreSQL"})," Many concurrent Go services would exhaust Postgres's connection limit, so all SQL goes through a PgBouncer pool. Trade-off: transaction-mode pooling is the safe default, but session-level features (server-side cursors, per-connection state) stop working across the pooler — queries have to stay pooler-friendly."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Full observability suite (Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger + Pyroscope + Alertmanager)"})," All three pillars plus continuous profiling, wired through OpenTelemetry — a slow transfer can be followed from the REST edge across gRPC boundaries down to SQL. The cost is a resident footprint of collectors and dashboards, justified only if someone actually operates them; in a payment system, alerting on ledger-state divergence and Kafka lag is exactly the part you'd never run without."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Docker Compose + Kubernetes as two first-class targets"})," Local parity with prod (same split, HPA manifests, PVCs) plus rolling updates/autoscaling from the orchestrator. The trade-off: two deployment artifacts that must stay in sync — compose and K8s manifests are where configuration drift lives, and both must be reviewed on every infra change."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"sqlc + Goose for the data layer"})," Type-safe, compiler-checked SQL and version-ordered migrations: predictable performance and no auto-migration surprises on a financial schema. The cost: every query is hand-written and a code-generation step sits between schema and code."]})," ",n(r.hr,{})," ",i(n.p,{children:[r(n.strong,{children:'Microservices at "simple" scale vs a monolith'}),"
Four domain services (user, product, order, role) plus a gateway — deliberately the lightest expression of the pattern. The cost of gRPC wiring, a Kafka broker, and the full observability suite on a single host exceeds what a monolith would need; the value is the pattern itself, as a baseline that the heavier e-commerce and payment-gateway variants build on."]}),"
",i(n.p,{children:[r(n.strong,{children:"gRPC internally + REST gateway at the edge"}),"
Typed, contract-first internal communication, while clients only ever see JSON + Swagger through the gateway. The trade-off: two interface layers to keep in sync, and error semantics are mapped twice — gRPC status codes have to be translated to HTTP codes at the gateway or clients see raw internal failures."]}),"
",i(n.p,{children:[r(n.strong,{children:"Kafka for asynchronous communication"}),'
Event-driven decoupling for order/notification flows: consumers can lag or restart without blocking a transaction. The costs: at-least-once delivery (consumers must be idempotent), ordering only within a partition, and a full broker in the compose file — real operational weight for a "simple" demo system.']}),"
",i(n.p,{children:[r(n.strong,{children:"sqlc + pgx for the data layer"}),"
Compiler-checked, type-safe Go code generated from hand-written SQL — no reflection, no ORM magic, and every query is explicit enough to audit with ",r(n.code,{children:"EXPLAIN"}),". The cost: every query is written by hand and a code-generation step sits between schema and code. At this service count, pgx's built-in pooler is sufficient for Postgres — the larger variant needed PgBouncer because socket exhaustion actually showed up; here it would have been a layer of indirection for nothing."]}),"
",i(n.p,{children:[r(n.strong,{children:"Load testing scope: read-only endpoints only"}),"
The published k6 numbers (capability/load/stress/spike per module) cover GET paths: that's where you cheaply establish a throughput baseline and backpressure behavior. The honest trade-off: the write path — checkout contention, order-item races — is the hardest part and is ",r(n.em,{children:"not"}),' measured in these results. Note the "dropped iterations" at the capability point is intentional backpressure protecting the service, not a failure; and single-node compose numbers do not transfer directly to a K8s deployment.']}),"

",n(r.h2,{id:"technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:n(r.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:"Technical Decisions & Trade-offs"})}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"True microservices with a database per service"}),"
Auth, user, role, product, order, and email each own a separate PostgreSQL database, so no service reaches into another's tables and every domain can evolve and scale independently. The cost is immediate: operations spanning services cannot share a transaction, so consistency becomes eventual and has to be designed rather than assumed. Operationally it is the heaviest option - a database, Redis, and deployment per service. That overhead is deliberate; the project exists to exercise the real pattern, not a cheap approximation of it."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Tonic gRPC between services"}),"
The internal protocol is typed proto contracts over HTTP/2, keeping cross-service calls fast and impossible to mismatch at compile time. The price is contract management - every change ripples through proto regeneration - and tooling, since debugging a gRPC hop needs dedicated clients where JSON can just be curled. The gateway is the only place that speaks plain REST."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"A gateway that owns rate limiting, sessions, and caching"}),"
External traffic enters through a single REST gateway that rate-limits, caches, and manages sessions before anything reaches the internal services. That shields the gRPC services from abusive or malformed traffic and keeps cross-cutting concerns in one place. The trade-off: the gateway is a bottleneck and a single point of failure by construction, and every request pays one extra hop. Concentrating that risk in one configurable layer beats exposing the internals."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"PgBouncer in front of every database"}),"
Independent services with their own connection pools can exhaust PostgreSQL quickly, because Postgres connections are expensive and services scale on their own schedules. PgBouncer caps and reuses connections so the databases stay healthy under fan-out. The cost is one more stateful component per database and pooling-mode constraints that trade away some session-level behavior."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Kafka for the asynchronous side of checkout"}),"
Order events go to Kafka and the email service consumes them, so the order flow completes without waiting on email delivery and an email outage cannot fail an order. The trade-offs are the standard event-driven ones: at-least-once delivery means consumers must be idempotent, and the broker is one more stateful service to run. Decoupling a side effect from the critical path is worth exactly that price."]}),"
",a(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Observability sized to the architecture"}),"
Seven services plus Kafka and multiple databases is where debugging by reading logs stops working, so observability is a first-class feature: OpenTelemetry to Jaeger for tracing, Prometheus and Node Exporter for metrics, Loki with Promtail for logs, and Alertmanager wired to Grafana. That is a lot of containers running before any business logic. The alternative - distributed debugging without traces - costs more the first time a request fails somewhere between the gateway and the order service."]}),"

title: Distributed Microservices — E-Commerce Platform (Spring Boot Cloud)

title: Distributed Microservices — E-Commerce Platform (Java Spring Boot + GraphQL)
excerpt: E-commerce microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6 with GraphQL API Gateway: catalog, cart, checkout, merchant suite, reviews, and transaction ledger as separate gRPC services. Kafka transactional outbox with DLQ, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Distributed Microservices — E-Commerce Platform (Java Spring Boot)
excerpt: E-commerce microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6: catalog, cart, checkout, merchant suite, reviews, and transaction ledger as separate gRPC services. Kafka transactional outbox with DLQ, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Distributed Microservices — E-Commerce Platform (Spring Boot + MongoDB + GraphQL)
excerpt: E-commerce microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6 with MongoDB and GraphQL API Gateway: catalog, cart, checkout, merchant suite, reviews, and transaction ledger as separate gRPC services. Kafka transactional outbox with DLQ, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Distributed Microservices — E-Commerce Platform (Spring Boot + MongoDB)
excerpt: E-commerce microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6 with MongoDB per bounded context: catalog, cart, checkout, merchant suite, reviews, and transaction ledger as separate gRPC services. Kafka transactional outbox with DLQ, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Distributed Microservices — Payment Gateway Platform (Spring Boot + MongoDB + GraphQL)
excerpt: Payment gateway microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6 with MongoDB and GraphQL API Gateway: card/VCC, balance, top-up, transfer, withdraw, and transaction ledger as separate gRPC services. Two-path fraud scoring, DLQ, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Distributed Microservices — Payment Gateway Platform (Spring Boot + MongoDB)
excerpt: Payment gateway microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6 with MongoDB: card/VCC, balance, top-up, transfer, withdraw, and transaction ledger as separate gRPC services. Two-path fraud scoring, DLQ, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Distributed Microservices — Point of Sale Platform (Spring Boot + MongoDB)
excerpt: Point-of-sale microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6 with MongoDB per bounded context: each domain becomes its own JVM process with its own gRPC server and Mongock migrations. Clean Architecture + CQRS, Kafka transactional outbox, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Distributed Microservices — Point of Sale Platform (Spring Boot + MongoDB)
excerpt: Point-of-sale microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6 with MongoDB per bounded context: each domain becomes its own JVM process with its own gRPC server and Mongock migrations. Clean Architecture + CQRS, Kafka transactional outbox, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Distributed Microservices — Payment Gateway Platform (Java Spring Boot)
excerpt: Payment gateway microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6: card/VCC, balance, top-up, transfer, withdraw, and transaction ledger as separate gRPC services. Two-path fraud scoring, DLQ, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Distributed Microservices — Payment Gateway Platform (Java Spring Boot)
excerpt: Payment gateway microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6: card/VCC, balance, top-up, transfer, withdraw, and transaction ledger as separate gRPC services. Two-path fraud scoring, DLQ, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Distributed Microservices — Point of Sale Platform (Java Spring Boot)
excerpt: Point-of-sale microservices backend in Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.6: each domain becomes its own JVM process with its own gRPC server, database, and Flyway. Clean Architecture + CQRS, Kafka transactional outbox, ClickHouse analytics, chaos engineering, and Kubernetes + ArgoCD GitOps.

title: Microservice Super App — Federated Go Domains with Kernel-Level Security
excerpt: A federated super-app backend: ERP, E-Commerce, Point of Sale, and Payment Gateway as autonomous domains bound together by a single edge gateway, a single Keycloak, a Kafka event backbone with outbox/inbox, cross-platform checkout sagas, a polyglot AI layer, and kernel-level security enforcement via eBPF XDP.

title: Microservice Superapp — Unified Vert.x Ecosystem (Java 21)
excerpt: Multi-platform superapp on the JVM: E-Commerce (20 modules), POS (11), Payment Gateway (11), and Quarkus ERP (17) behind a single Unified API Gateway and Kafka KRaft. Non-blocking I/O, CQRS, transactional outbox, cross-platform payment sagas, and eBPF kernel security (XDP + Sigma) without application instrumentation.

items.title: ERD — Point of Sale (cashier and transactions)
How the unified gateway reaches the ERP
1. Build the shared library and core services
eBPF runtime security — two components with distinct roles
ebpf-observability — runtime detection and TCP telemetry (:9095)
ebpf-firewall — XDP enforcement and control plane (:9096, :9097)
Synchronous — HTTP to gRPC to database

Trade-offs"})})," ",a(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"Go with assembled libraries vs a batteries-included framework"})," Go buys small static binaries, fast startup, and cheap concurrency — at 21 independently deployable services, that footprint difference is what makes the full stack runnable on a single machine at all. The cost is that nothing comes bundled: auth, logging, resilience, and database plumbing are hand-assembled from Echo, Zap, sqlc, and the shared pkg modules rather than provided by a framework. For a project whose point is understanding the plumbing, that is a feature, not a defect."]})," ",a(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"Distributed modular monolith vs one process"})," Each domain ships as its own container with isolated data access, but everything still shares one codebase, one set of protobuf contracts, and one PostgreSQL instance. The honest cost of the split: a checkout can no longer be a single ACID transaction, because the order, its items, and the payment status live behind different gRPC boundaries — consistency becomes an application concern handled through status tracking and Kafka-driven confirmation pipelines instead of a database guarantee. A true single binary would be simpler to reason about; a full microservice organization would not share this much. This sits deliberately in between."]})," ",a(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"gRPC and Protobuf behind a REST gateway"})," Contract-first protobuf keeps the service interfaces typed and reviewable, and generated code catches drift at compile time across all 21 domains. The price: browsers speak JSON, so every external request pays a translation hop through the Echo API gateway, and each schema change means regenerating proto definitions, mappers, and stubs before any logic can move. At this service count the contract discipline pays for itself; at three services it would feel like ceremony."]})," ",a(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"sqlc over an ORM"})," Queries are written as SQL and compiled into type-safe Go, so there is no hidden lazy loading, no surprise N+1 across products, carts, and order items, and the exact statement hitting PostgreSQL is always visible. The trade-off is verbosity: relationships must be joined by hand, dynamic queries get awkward, and every new query is a codegen step. For read-heavy catalog and cart paths, predictability beats convenience."]})," ",a(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"JWT at the edge, permissions cached in Redis"})," Stateless tokens let the gateway authenticate once and forward identity over gRPC, which fits the HPA-driven scaling story without session affinity. The weakness is revocation — a leaked token stays valid until expiry — and role permissions cached in Redis add a staleness window on top, so a revoked permission can linger until invalidation runs. Acceptable for this threat model; a real deployment would shorten TTLs before trusting it."]})," ",a(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"Stock integrity across the checkout path (the core domain risk)"})," Stock tracking lives in the product service while orders are created by the order service, so a decrement cannot share the order's database transaction. The failure modes are overselling (two concurrent checkouts pass the same availability check) and orphaned decrements (the order fails after stock was reserved), and the mitigation — a conditional check-and-decrement inside the product service plus compensation events when an order fails — is strictly more machinery than the single update a monolith would run. That extra machinery is the actual price of the modular split, and it is the first place this architecture would break under load."]})," ",n(l.hr,{})," ",n(l.h2,{id:"getting-started",children:n(l.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#getting-started",children:"Getting Started"})})," ",n(l.h3,{id:"prerequisites",children:n(l.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#prerequisites",children:"Prerequisites"})})," ",n(l.p,{children:"Ensure the following tools are installed on your system:"})," ",a(l.ul,{children:[" ",n(l.li,{children:n(l.a,{href:"https://git-scm.com/",children:"Git"})})," ",a(l.li,{children:[n(l.a,{href:"https://go.dev/",children:"Go"})," (v1.20+)"]})," ",a(l.li,{children:[n(l.a,{href:"https://www.docker.com/",children:"Docker"})," & ",n(l.a,{href:"https://docs.docker.com/compose/",children:"Docker Compose"})]})," ",a(l.li,{children:[n(l.a,{href:"https://www.gnu.org/software/make/",children:"Make"})," or ",n(l.a,{href:"https://github.com/casey/just",children:"Just"})," (task runner)"]})," ",a(l.li,{children:[n(l.a,{href:"https://grpc.io/docs/protoc-installation/",children:"Protobuf Compiler"})," (for proto generation)"]})," "]})," ",n(l.h3,{id:"1-clone-the-repository",children:n(l.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#1-clone-the-repository",children:"1. ",i(r.p,{children:[a(r.strong,{children:"FastAPI for money-moving endpoints"}),"
Async request handling plus Pydantic-validated bodies put strict typing on exactly the surface where malformed input hurts most: top-ups, transfers, withdrawals. The cost is assembling the rest yourself — auth, ORM wiring, and background workers are all manual compared to a batteries-included framework, and the GIL still caps CPU-bound work per process even though this I/O-heavy workload barely notices it."]}),"
",i(r.p,{children:[a(r.strong,{children:"Monolith first, services later"}),"
Keeping balance, top-up, transfer, withdrawal, and email in one deployable means a transfer can be validated and settled in a single database transaction — no sagas, no distributed commit choreography. The trade: a bug in the email path can take the transfer path down with it, and module boundaries survive through discipline rather than deployment isolation. At this size, correctness beats independence."]}),"
",i(r.p,{children:[a(r.strong,{children:"Kafka for notifications, not for money movement"}),"
Emails ride Kafka so SMTP latency never lands in a transfer's response time. The discipline this forces: Kafka is at-least-once, so a redelivered message must not read as a second top-up — the ledger stays the source of truth while the notification stream is treated as best-effort, duplicates allowed."]}),"
",i(r.p,{children:[a(r.strong,{children:"Tracing from day one"}),"
OpenTelemetry spans across every service, collected in Jaeger, turn a slow balance query into a searchable trace instead of a support ticket. ",n(t.h2,{id:"technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:n(t.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:"Technical Decisions & Trade-offs"})}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Modular monolith with a shared database"}),"
Users, balances, and transactions live in separate crates that talk over gRPC, but all of them read and write one PostgreSQL database. The upside is financial integrity: a transfer or withdrawal touching several domains runs in a single local transaction, with no sagas or two-phase commit. The downside is coupling - every crate is bound to the same schema, and splitting into true microservices later means untangling the data first. For a gateway at this scale, shared data with enforced code-level boundaries is the honest choice."]}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Rust and tokio for the runtime"}),"
No garbage collector means no unpredictable latency spikes, which matters when the endpoint is moving money. The price is paid up front: the borrow checker rejects designs a GC language would accept, and a workspace of this size means noticeable compile times on every change. Predictable tail latency is worth the slower iteration in this domain."]}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"Tonic and prost for the internal contracts"}),"
Protocol Buffers are the single source of truth for what each module exposes, and generated types turn mismatched calls into compile errors. The cost is a codegen step in every build and a less forgiving workflow than passing JSON around. When money is on the line, contracts that cannot silently drift are the better default."]}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"SQLx with compile-time checked queries"}),"
Queries are validated against the live schema at build time, so a renamed column breaks the build instead of the payment flow. The trade-off is that SQL lives as strings in the code: no entity relations or query builder, and anything dynamic gets verbose. For a gateway with a stable, well-defined schema, that is an acceptable price for the safety."]}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"One React codebase for web and desktop via Tauri"}),"
The dashboard is React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind, and Tauri wraps the same build into a desktop application with a Rust shell. One frontend instead of two is a real maintenance saving. The cost is that the desktop target ties releases to a Rust toolchain, and Tauri is a thinner ecosystem than Electron when native quirks appear."]}),"
",r(t.p,{children:[n(t.strong,{children:"k6 load testing as a published artifact"}),"
The repository documents smoke, capability, load, stress, and spike results per module, including where the system intentionally degrades around 1500 virtual users. binaries plus gRPC's binary protobuf payloads deliver predictable round-trips that generated client stubs can be built against. The cost is framework absence: auth, logging, and resilience come from the shared pkg modules instead of a batteries-included stack, and protobuf contracts add a regeneration step to every interface change. For an API that cashier and merchant clients integrate against, contract-first is worth the ceremony."]})," ",r(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"Splitting the checkout across four services"})," Order, order item, product, and transaction each run as their own container, so the transaction service can scale independently for peak hours and a catalog bug does not take sales down with it. The price shows up exactly at checkout: creating an order, decomposing items, and recording payment cross three gRPC boundaries where a single-deployable POS would use one database transaction. The isolation is real, and so is the consistency work it pushes into application code."]})," ",r(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"Redis in the read path"})," Product lookups and role permissions are served cache-first with instrumented hit ratios, which keeps the catalog off PostgreSQL during a rush. The trade-off is staleness: a price or stock change does not reach the register until invalidation lands, so anything the till depends on for correctness — stock especially — must be re-checked against the database at write time rather than trusted from cache."]})," ",r(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"JWT roles for staff hardware"})," Stateless tokens suit register clients that reconnect often and cannot require session affinity, and the RBAC model keeps a cashier token away from merchant and admin operations. The gap is revocation: deactivating a cashier mid-shift does not kill an already-issued token until expiry, so the practical mitigation is short access-token lifetimes backed by refresh rotation. Contained for internal staff devices, but a real limit to design around."]})," ",r(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"Kafka-decoupled notifications"})," Transaction and merchant events flow to the email service asynchronously, so a slow SMTP provider cannot stall a sale. The cost is eventual consistency and at-least-once delivery — consumers must tolerate duplicates, and consumer lag becomes a health metric worth exporting rather than a silent backlog."]})," ",r(l.p,{children:[n(l.strong,{children:"Cashier attribution and stock integrity (the core domain risk)"})," The cashier service tracks per-cashier status and monthly or yearly sales performance, which only means anything if every order and transaction carries its cashier identity and failed payments are persisted as records instead of dropped — otherwise end-of-day reconciliation quietly falls apart. On the inventory side, stock tracking lives in the product service while checkout runs in the order service, so the check-and-decrement cannot share one transaction; without a conditional update there, two simultaneous sales of the last unit can both succeed. That is the price of layering GraphQL over contract-first services instead of a dedicated data layer."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Quarkus reactive runtime over Spring Boot"})," The reactive engine keeps gateway threads free while one query fans out to several downstream modules at once, which is exactly the workload a GraphQL resolver creates. For a gateway whose job is concurrent fan-out, the reactive model fits."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"PostgreSQL 17 with PgBouncer and Flyway"})," Cart, order, and transaction data demand ACID semantics, and the audit-ledger design depends on relational integrity holding across every module. The costs are pooled-connection ceilings under burst load and a fixed schema shared across all 21 modules."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Kafka-driven invoice and notification worker"})," Order and transaction events are published to Kafka and the email worker handles SMTP on its own clock, so a slow mail server never delays checkout. locks"})," Balance writes use optimistic locking, so concurrent debits do not queue behind database row locks and throughput stays high under normal traffic. The cost appears on hot accounts: contended updates fail and the service layer must retry, and a genuinely popular card could turn that into visible latency. For this workload the lock-free path wins, with the transaction ledger capturing every attempt either way."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Transfer as a multi-module flow, not a distributed transaction"})," A card-to-card transfer is sequenced through the card, saldo, and transaction services over gRPC; no transaction manager spans them. The upside is that modules stay independently evolvable; the downside is that a failure mid-sequence can leave a debit without its matching credit. Status tracking in the centralized transaction ledger is the reconciliation surface, a deliberate bet that operational reconciliation beats bolting on saga orchestration."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Soft delete and restore for financial records"})," Cards, merchants, and topup records are marked deleted rather than removed, so history survives operator error and audits can be replayed. The bill arrives as query complexity, since every read must filter tombstones, and as unbounded table growth. For money movement, never physically destroying records is the cheaper regret."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Caching balances with Redis, carefully"})," The saldo service keeps a Redis-side copy for fast reads, which keeps dashboards and card screens responsive under load. The trade-off is that a cached balance can briefly trail the ledger, so staleness is only tolerated on the read path; anything that actually moves money is validated by optimistic locking against PostgreSQL at write time. Knowing that boundary is what makes caching money safe."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Withdraw thresholds instead of a fraud engine"})," Daily transaction limits on withdrawals are a blunt but cheap risk control: no external scoring service, no model to maintain, just a hard ceiling on blast radius. The trade-off is coarse edges, since legitimate heavy users get blocked while determined fraud is merely slowed down. A gateway whose core job is concurrent fan-out is exactly where that model pays off."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Checkout and receipt integrity"})," An order mutation reaches the product service for price and stock state and the transaction service for the audit register, and nothing wraps those calls in one atomic transaction. Consistency therefore rests on the flow: order items decompose the basket with the prices looked up at checkout, and the centralized transaction ledger is the record to reconcile against if a step fails. Module isolation buys clean ownership and charges for it in coordination logic."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Caching the catalog, not the sale"})," Redis absorbs product and permission reads so browsing and search stay fast under load, while the checkout flow performs its price lookup through the product service instead of trusting a cached value. In point of sale, a stale price is not a performance issue, it is a correctness bug."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"Kafka-driven receipts and notifications"})," Completed orders publish events and a dedicated email worker sends receipts and invoices, so SMTP problems can never make a customer wait at the register. At-least-once delivery means duplicate receipt emails are possible without deduplication, and the broker is one more thing to run. Offloading receipt delivery from the checkout path is worth both."]})," ",l(r.p,{children:[n(r.strong,{children:"PostgreSQL 17, PgBouncer, and Flyway migrations"})," Sales ledgers, order items, and inventory counts need ACID transactions and relational integrity, so the database choice was settled before the architecture was. ",n(a.h2,{id:"technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:n(a.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:"Technical Decisions & Trade-offs"})}),"
",r(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Modular monolith instead of full microservices"}),"
Each domain (auth, user, role, product, order, email) is an isolated crate with its own gRPC API, but the whole system ships and deploys as one unit behind a single gateway. That buys real service boundaries and explicit contracts without the operational tax of independently deployed microservices. The cost is that some boundaries are ceremony at this scale: calling a function over the network is slower and more verbose than calling it in-process, and the proto definitions are extra surface to maintain. It is the right middle ground for exercising the pattern while keeping ",n(a.code,{children:"docker compose up"})," as the entire deployment story."]}),"
",r(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Tonic gRPC for inter-service communication"}),"
Typed proto contracts make every internal call compile-checked on both ends, and HTTP/2 multiplexing keeps the hop cheap. The trade-off is iteration friction: changing a message means regenerating the prost code and updating every client, and a failing gRPC call is harder to inspect than a JSON payload. REST exists only at the Axum gateway, so the stricter protocol stays on the internal network where it pays off."]}),"
",r(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Axum as the public REST gateway"}),"
External clients get plain JSON over HTTP, and the gateway doubles as a load balancer in front of the internal services. The price is an extra network hop on every request plus a second framework to maintain. Concentrating authentication, routing, and client-facing concerns at one edge is worth it - the alternative is every client knowing the internal service topology."]}),"
",r(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Kafka for order events"}),"
Order completion is published to Kafka and consumed by the email worker, so checkout is never blocked on sending mail and the order service knows nothing about email. The cost is a stateful broker in the stack and at-least-once delivery, which forces consumers to tolerate duplicates. For an event-driven design lesson built into the domain, that complexity is the point."]}),"
",r(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"SQLx over a full ORM"}),"
Queries are written as SQL and checked against the real schema at compile time, with sqlx-cli handling migrations. That catches broken queries at build time, which is exactly where an ORM without compile-time checking gives you nothing. The cost is less abstraction: no entity graph or relation API, so complex result mapping is manual and SQL strings live in the source."]}),"
",r(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Observability from day one"}),"
OpenTelemetry feeds Jaeger, Prometheus, and Loki, so a request crossing five services can be followed end to end. The stack is a heavy docker-compose footprint for a portfolio project and demands real learning time. But in a distributed design, debugging without traces and correlated logs is guesswork, so this is load-bearing infrastructure rather than decoration."]}),"

",i(a.li,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"User"}),": Sends requests (for example, registration, transfer, top-up) through the REST API to the ",n(a.code,{children:"Client Service"}),"."]}),"
",i(a.li,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Client Service (Axum)"}),": Receives HTTP requests, performs initial validation, and forwards them to the ",n(a.code,{children:"Server Service"})," via gRPC calls."]}),"
",i(a.li,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Server Service (Tonic)"}),": Receives gRPC calls, processes all business logic, interacts with the database (PostgreSQL) and cache (Redis), then returns the result."]}),"
",i(a.li,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Database (PostgreSQL)"}),": Stores persistent data such as user information, balances, and transaction history."]}),"
",i(a.li,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Observability"}),": Metrics from both services are collected by Prometheus, and logs are collected by Loki. Both can be visualized using Grafana."]}),"
"]}),"
",n(a.h2,{id:"technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:n(a.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#technical-decisions--trade-offs",children:"Technical Decisions & Trade-offs"})}),"
",i(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"A monorepo split into a public REST edge and a private gRPC core"}),"
One workspace holds two services: an Axum client that validates and forwards external requests, and a Tonic server that owns the money logic. The split enforces a real boundary - the edge never touches the database directly - while a single repository keeps the proto contracts and both services in lockstep. The cost is a network hop plus serialization on every call that a single binary would not pay, and two deployables to run even in development. At this scale that overhead is paid deliberately, to keep the separation honest."]}),"
",i(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"SeaQuery for dynamic queries, SQLx for execution"}),"
Filters and query shapes are composed programmatically with SeaQuery instead of concatenated SQL strings, then run through SQLx's pool, with migrations handled by sqlx-cli. The benefit is injection-safe, composable queries; the cost is two query layers to understand and generated SQL that occasionally needs inspecting before you trust it. For a payment schema with many filtered list endpoints, the composability earns its keep."]}),"
",i(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Tonic gRPC as the internal contract"}),"
Protocol Buffers define the interface between client and server, so mismatches fail at compile time and payloads stay compact. The trade-off is workflow friction: contract changes mean proto regeneration in the shared crate, and debugging needs gRPC-specific tooling. Inside a monorepo the regeneration step is cheap, which is where this design is most comfortable."]}),"
",i(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Axum and utoipa on the public edge"}),"
The REST side speaks the HTTP and JSON that web and mobile clients expect, with OpenAPI documentation generated from the handlers. The cost is maintaining two views of the same operations - REST at the edge, gRPC in the core - and keeping the OpenAPI annotations truthful. Exposing REST externally while keeping the typed protocol internal is the standard shape for good reason."]}),"
",i(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Redis in front of PostgreSQL"}),"
Sessions and hot reads are served from Redis so the database is not hit for every token check. The trade-offs are cache invalidation and a second stateful service that can fail independently. At this traffic level Redis is more learning exercise than necessity - which is a fair thing for a project like this to be."]}),"
",i(a.p,{children:[n(a.strong,{children:"Database transactions for money movement"}),"
Transfers debit and credit inside one SQLx transaction against PostgreSQL, so a partial move can never be committed. The boundary of that guarantee is the single database: scaling writes eventually means distributing the transaction, which is a genuinely hard problem. One honest gap is retry safety - idempotency keys on the mutating endpoints - which this example does not implement."]}),"

body:
const{Fragment:e,jsx:a,jsxs:t}=arguments[0];function _createMdxContent(n){const r={a:"a",code:"code",figure:"figure",h2:"h2",h3:"h3",li:"li",p:"p",pre:"pre",span:"span",strong:"strong",ul:"ul",...n.components};return t(e,{children:[a(r.h2,{id:"tech-stack",children:a(r.a,{className:"subheading-anchor","aria-label":"Link to section",href:"#tech-stack",children:"Tech Stack"})}),"
